text: Hello, this is Grete. Annemarie is alone on the path with the basket, and she hears something ahead of her. This is the chapter the whole book has been building toward. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 15, and study one sentence the way a writer does. Today’s question: when the soldiers stop her, what does she do?

Today’s reading move: hold one detail up to a fact. Pick one thing from this chapter, like the dogs, or soldiers stopping a child, and turn it into a question a history book could answer. Write the question down. You’re not trying to catch Lowry out. You’re finding where the history ends and the storytelling begins.

The model is a plain sentence about a soldier’s question. The sentence to fix has three sound-alike words, and every one of them is the wrong twin. One should be a number, one should show belonging, and one should mean very. Then find where the first thought ends, and give the sentence a stop.

Last time you found sound-alike words. This time, some of them are wrong. In grammar and spelling, you’re hunting for the twin that slipped into the wrong sentence. Read slowly. A wrong twin sounds perfect when you say it, and that is exactly why it’s so easy to miss.

More windows are waiting on the street. Today’s words all take one of the three roots again. One of them is a word for something your body does before you can even think about it. Ask what each word is about, a shape or bending, and then light the window.

Quick match today. You met these four words in the last lesson, so try to match them without looking back. Then see if you can find a moment in Chapter 15 where Annemarie has to conform, to fit the shape of what the soldiers expect to see.

Every sound-alike word in this paragraph might be right, or it might be the wrong twin. Tap only the wrong ones. Read each one and ask what it has to mean in that spot. A place? Belonging? A number, or very? The meaning decides, not the sound.

This is the same kind of hunt. Some of these words are the wrong twin, and your ear will tell you everything is fine. Don’t trust it. Look at each word. Then pick one you tapped, spell it the right way, and say what the wrong word really means.

Today’s Courage Watch is about courage that looks silly. Once, when soldiers stopped my father’s cart, my mother chattered about the weather and laughed too loudly. I was embarrassed. Later I understood: she was keeping their eyes on her, not on the sacks behind us. Watch Annemarie. Sometimes the bravest thing is to seem like nothing at all.

Read this chapter slowly. It’s short, and almost all of it happens in one place, on the path, with the soldiers in front of her. Notice what Annemarie says, and what she lets them see. Notice the dogs, too: where they look, and what they want. And at the very end, watch which way the soldiers go.

This sentence sends the soldiers away, back down the path toward where Annemarie came from. It adds nothing new, and that’s the point. It closes the scene by circling back to where it began. When you write your own, end a moment by pointing it home, back toward the start.

Now you write. The questions ask what Annemarie does when the dogs sniff the basket, what the chapter keeps secret about the handkerchief, and how this scene compares with the real rescue. Then you revise your essay by reading it out loud and fixing whatever makes your tongue trip.

The second question is about a mystery Lowry chooses not to explain yet. Don’t guess too hard at the answer. Think instead about why an author would hold something back. What does not knowing do to you as a reader, right here, on this page?

Revision is for the ear. Read your whole essay out loud, slowly, the way you’d read it to someone else. If your tongue trips, the sentence is too long. If you hear one word three times, swap one out. If a sentence sounds flat, find a stronger verb. Spelling can wait for the next lesson.

There was a dog on our street during the war, a shaggy farm dog who barked at everyone. The soldiers’ dogs were different. They were quiet, and they watched. I remember one standing beside a truck, ears up, nose working. I didn’t know then what those noses could find. Annemarie is about to meet two of them.
Perform. To carry out, all the way through.
Reflex. A quick move your body makes without thinking.
Deform. To spoil the shape of something. Eight windows are lit.
